title: URL Shortener
summary: Create short links with fast, reliable redirects and manageable abuse controls.
prompt: Design a service that lets users create short links and redirects visitors to the original destinations.
clarifyingQuestions: Are custom aliases and expiration required?
Is redirect latency more important than link-creation latency?
Do links need editing, analytics, or deletion?
What abuse and unsafe-destination controls belong in scope?
functionalRequirements: Create a short code for a valid destination URL.
Redirect a short code to its current destination.
Support optional expiration and owner-managed deletion.
nonFunctionalRequirements: Redirects should remain available during partial service failure.
The read-heavy path should have predictable low latency.
A code must never resolve to two different active links.
scaleAssumptions: Example interview assumption: 10 million active links are created per month.
Example interview assumption: redirects outnumber creations by roughly 100 to 1.
State the desired link-retention period before sizing storage.
capacityDiscussion: Estimate redirects per second from the hypothetical read/write ratio, then add a peak factor.
Estimate URL-record storage separately from click analytics, which can grow much faster.
Use cache hit rate to reason about database read pressure rather than assuming every redirect is cached.

coreComponents.name: Link API
coreComponents.purpose: Validates requests, allocates codes, and persists mappings.

coreComponents.name: Redirect service
coreComponents.purpose: Resolves codes on the latency-sensitive read path.

coreComponents.name: Mapping store
coreComponents.purpose: Owns the durable code-to-destination record.

coreComponents.name: Cache
coreComponents.purpose: Keeps frequently visited mappings close to redirect workers.

dataModelNotes: A link record can key by short code and store destination, owner, state, and expiration.
Code allocation may use random tokens, range allocation, or an encoded unique ID; compare collision and predictability concerns.
Keep high-volume click events outside the transactional mapping row.
apiNotes: POST /links accepts a destination and optional alias or expiration.
GET /{code} returns an HTTP redirect or a stable not-found/expired response.
DELETE /links/{code} should require ownership and be idempotent.
keyTradeoffs: Random codes reduce coordination but require collision handling; sequential IDs simplify uniqueness but may reveal volume.
Cache-aside is simple, while a write-through path can reduce first-read misses at higher write complexity.
Permanent redirects improve caching but make destination changes harder to propagate.
failureModes: Cache outage sends a sudden read surge to storage.
A code-allocation bug produces collisions or uneven shards.
Expired or deleted mappings remain in caches after state changes.
Abusive destinations overwhelm review or reputation services.
extensions: How would you add regional redirects?
How would privacy-preserving aggregate analytics work?
What changes if custom aliases must be globally unique?
interviewChecklist: Estimated the read-heavy path using stated assumptions.
Chose a code strategy and collision policy.
Explained cache invalidation and storage failure behavior.
Separated core redirects from optional analytics.

title: Notification Service
summary: Deliver user notifications across channels with preferences, retries, and observable outcomes.
prompt: Design a service that accepts notification requests and delivers them through email, push, and SMS while respecting user preferences.
clarifyingQuestions: Which channels and delivery guarantees are required?
Are notifications transactional, promotional, or both?
How quickly must each priority class be delivered?
Who owns templates, localization, and quiet hours?
functionalRequirements: Accept a notification intent with recipient, template, and variables.
Resolve preferences and eligible channels.
Track channel attempts and terminal outcomes.
Support cancellation before dispatch when feasible.
nonFunctionalRequirements: A provider slowdown must not block unrelated channels.
Duplicate requests should not create duplicate user-visible sends.
Priority traffic should retain capacity during bulk campaigns.
scaleAssumptions: Example interview assumption: 50 million notification intents per day.
Assume traffic is bursty around product events rather than uniform.
Define retention separately for delivery state and long-term reporting.
capacityDiscussion: Convert daily volume into baseline and peak queue ingress.
Size worker pools by per-provider throughput and latency, not only global volume.
Estimate retry amplification during a provider incident and enforce retry budgets.

coreComponents.name: Notification API
coreComponents.purpose: Validates and durably accepts notification intents.

coreComponents.name: Orchestrator
coreComponents.purpose: Applies preference, template, and channel policy.

coreComponents.name: Channel queues
coreComponents.purpose: Isolate email, push, and SMS workloads.

coreComponents.name: Delivery workers
coreComponents.purpose: Call providers and record normalized outcomes.

coreComponents.name: Status store
coreComponents.purpose: Tracks intent and attempt lifecycle.

dataModelNotes: Separate immutable notification intent from channel delivery attempts.
Use an idempotency key scoped to the caller and business action.
Version templates so retries render the intended content.
apiNotes: POST /notifications returns an accepted intent ID after durable enqueue.
GET /notifications/{id} returns aggregate state and channel attempts.
Provider callbacks require authentication and deduplication.
keyTradeoffs: At-least-once delivery with idempotent effects is practical; exactly-once claims are not.
Fan-out on write improves delivery latency but creates more queued work.
A shared provider adapter simplifies policy while channel-specific services improve isolation.
failureModes: Provider timeouts trigger a retry storm.
Preference data is unavailable at dispatch time.
A poison template repeatedly fails one queue partition.
Provider callbacks arrive late, duplicated, or out of order.
extensions: How would scheduled delivery work?
How would you support per-tenant quotas?
How should a global provider outage change product behavior?
interviewChecklist: Explained status observability and provider failure.

title: Chat System
summary: Support durable conversations, real-time delivery, ordering, and multi-device synchronization.
prompt: Design a chat service for direct and small-group conversations with online delivery and offline synchronization.
clarifyingQuestions: What is the maximum group size?
Are typing, presence, read receipts, and attachments in scope?
What ordering guarantee do users expect?
How long is message history retained?
functionalRequirements: Create conversations and manage membership.
Send and receive text messages in near real time.
Sync missed messages across multiple devices.
Expose delivery and read state if included.
nonFunctionalRequirements: Acknowledged messages should be durable.
Ordering should be defined per conversation rather than globally.
Connection loss must recover without silent gaps.
scaleAssumptions: Example interview assumption: 5 million concurrent connections at peak.
Assume small groups dominate and very large broadcast rooms are out of scope.
Estimate stored messages from active users, messages per day, payload size, and retention.
capacityDiscussion: Separate persistent connection capacity from message write throughput.
Account for fan-out: one accepted group message can produce several device deliveries.
Use a cursor or sequence to estimate offline-sync read patterns.

coreComponents.name: Connection gateways
coreComponents.purpose: Hold authenticated long-lived client connections.

coreComponents.name: Message service
coreComponents.purpose: Validates membership and durably appends messages.

coreComponents.name: Conversation store
coreComponents.purpose: Stores ordered message history and membership.

coreComponents.name: Delivery bus
coreComponents.purpose: Routes new-message events to connected recipients.

coreComponents.name: Sync API
coreComponents.purpose: Returns messages after a device cursor.

dataModelNotes: Partition messages by conversation to keep common reads and ordering local.
Assign a monotonic conversation sequence after durable acceptance.
Store per-user or per-device cursors separately from message bodies.
apiNotes: POST /conversations/{id}/messages accepts a client idempotency key.
GET /conversations/{id}/messages?after=cursor supports bounded sync.
A bidirectional connection carries new messages and acknowledgements.
keyTradeoffs: Server-assigned sequence simplifies ordering but adds coordination within a conversation shard.
Fan-out on write speeds inbox reads but is expensive for large groups.
Presence can be ephemeral and approximate while message durability cannot.
failureModes: A gateway disconnects and clients miss transient pushes.
A hot group overloads one conversation partition.
Duplicate sends appear after client retries.
Membership changes race with message delivery.
extensions: How would attachments change the architecture?
How would end-to-end encryption affect search and multi-device sync?
How would very large channels be handled separately?
interviewChecklist: Separated connection state from durable message state.

title: Distributed Rate Limiter
summary: Protect services with explicit quotas while balancing accuracy, availability, and cost.
prompt: Design a distributed rate-limiting service that enforces configurable request quotas for APIs.
clarifyingQuestions: What identities can be limited: user, token, IP, tenant, or route?
Must limits be exact across regions?
What happens if the limiter is unavailable?
How quickly must configuration changes propagate?
functionalRequirements: Evaluate an admission request against one or more rules.
Return allow or deny plus remaining quota metadata where useful.
Support versioned policy updates and scoped exceptions.
nonFunctionalRequirements: The decision path must add little latency.
A hot identity must not destabilize unrelated keys.
Failure behavior must be explicit for protected and noncritical routes.
scaleAssumptions: Example interview assumption: the limiter evaluates one million requests per second globally.
Assume most keys are cold while a small number receive heavy bursts.
Define required accuracy and regional topology before sizing coordination.
capacityDiscussion: Estimate decision operations and memory from active keys per window.
Compare centralized counters with local token leasing to reduce cross-region calls.
Bound key cardinality and expiration to prevent unbounded state.

coreComponents.name: Policy service
coreComponents.purpose: Stores and distributes versioned quota rules.

coreComponents.name: Decision nodes
coreComponents.purpose: Evaluate requests near the protected service.

coreComponents.name: Counter store
coreComponents.purpose: Maintains shared or leased quota state.

coreComponents.name: Telemetry pipeline
coreComponents.purpose: Reports denies, saturation, and policy errors.

dataModelNotes: A counter key should include policy version, identity scope, and time bucket or token state.
Expire inactive keys automatically.
Keep policy configuration separate from high-frequency counters.
apiNotes: CHECK accepts identity dimensions, route, cost, and request ID.
The response includes allowed, retry-after, and matched policy version.
Policy writes require validation and staged rollout.
keyTradeoffs: Fixed windows are simple but burst at boundaries; token buckets model sustained rate plus burst capacity.
Global accuracy requires coordination, while regional limits reduce latency and improve isolation.
Fail-open protects availability; fail-closed protects scarce or security-sensitive resources.
failureModes: Counter storage latency blocks the request path.
A cardinality attack creates excessive keys.
Clock skew distorts window boundaries.
Stale policy remains active on a subset of decision nodes.
extensions: How would hierarchical tenant and user quotas combine?
How would weighted requests consume different costs?
How would you migrate policies without resetting counters?
interviewChecklist: Explained fail-open or fail-closed per route.
Handled hot keys and state expiration.

title: News Feed
summary: Assemble a personalized feed with scalable fan-out, ranking boundaries, and freshness controls.
prompt: Design a home feed that shows recent posts from accounts a user follows, with room for later ranking.
clarifyingQuestions: Is the first version chronological or ranked?
How large can follower graphs become?
What freshness and pagination behavior is expected?
Are edits, deletions, privacy changes, and blocks in scope?
functionalRequirements: Publish posts and follow or unfollow accounts.
Read a paginated home feed.
Remove inaccessible content after delete or privacy changes.
nonFunctionalRequirements: Feed reads should be fast for typical users.
Celebrity publishers must not create unbounded synchronous fan-out.
Pagination should avoid obvious duplicates and gaps.
scaleAssumptions: Example interview assumption: 20 million daily readers and 2 million daily publishers.
Model follower-degree distribution instead of using only an average.
Assume a bounded recent-feed horizon for precomputed inbox entries.
capacityDiscussion: Estimate post writes, feed reads, and fan-out writes as separate workloads.
Use the follower distribution to identify a threshold for hybrid fan-out.
Estimate cache and inbox storage from active users times retained feed entries.

coreComponents.name: Post service
coreComponents.purpose: Stores canonical posts and visibility state.

coreComponents.name: Graph service
coreComponents.purpose: Owns follow relationships and graph queries.

coreComponents.name: Fan-out workers
coreComponents.purpose: Materialize feed references for ordinary publishers.

coreComponents.name: Feed service
coreComponents.purpose: Merges inbox entries and pull-based high-degree publishers.

coreComponents.name: Feed cache
coreComponents.purpose: Keeps recent assembled pages close to readers.

dataModelNotes: Store canonical post content separately from feed references.
Partition feed inboxes by reader ID and posts by author or post ID.
Use opaque cursors tied to ordering keys rather than numeric page offsets.
apiNotes: POST /posts durably stores before asynchronous distribution.
GET /feed?cursor=... returns references hydrated against current visibility.
Follow changes should define whether old posts appear retroactively.
keyTradeoffs: Fan-out on write gives fast reads but creates amplification; fan-out on read shifts cost to request time.
A hybrid model treats high-degree publishers differently.
Precomputation improves latency but requires delete and privacy repair paths.
failureModes: Fan-out lag makes new posts appear late.
A celebrity post overloads queues.
Deleted or blocked content remains in materialized inboxes.
Cursor semantics produce duplicate items during concurrent publication.
extensions: Where would an ML ranker fit?
How would promoted content be isolated and audited?
How would multi-region posting affect feed order?
interviewChecklist: Separated canonical posts from feed references.
Handled privacy repair and stable pagination.

title: Cloud File Storage
summary: Store large files, synchronize metadata, and support resumable transfer and sharing.
prompt: Design a cloud file service where users upload, download, organize, and share files across devices.
clarifyingQuestions: What file-size limits and sharing modes are required?
Is version history in scope?
Must multiple users edit the same file?
What sync latency is acceptable across devices?
functionalRequirements: Upload and download large files with resume support.
Create folders, rename items, and manage sharing permissions.
Synchronize metadata changes and optional file versions across devices.
nonFunctionalRequirements: Acknowledged file versions must be durable.
Large transfers should bypass application servers where safe.
Authorization must be checked independently from possession of an internal object key.
scaleAssumptions: Example interview assumption: 50 million users with highly variable storage footprints.
Assume file bytes dominate metadata by several orders of magnitude.
Estimate upload bandwidth and object storage separately from metadata operations.
capacityDiscussion: Use multipart chunk size and concurrent uploads to estimate transfer-service work.
Estimate metadata rows from files, versions, and sharing edges.
Discuss deduplication only after clarifying privacy and encryption boundaries.

coreComponents.name: Metadata API
coreComponents.purpose: Owns hierarchy, versions, permissions, and upload sessions.

coreComponents.name: Object storage
coreComponents.purpose: Stores immutable file bytes or chunks.

coreComponents.name: Transfer service
coreComponents.purpose: Issues scoped upload and download URLs and validates completion.

coreComponents.name: Change journal
coreComponents.purpose: Provides ordered metadata changes for device sync.

coreComponents.name: CDN
coreComponents.purpose: Accelerates eligible downloads without bypassing authorization policy.

dataModelNotes: Represent each file version as immutable object metadata pointing to object storage.
Folders are metadata relationships, not physical object-store directories.
Use a journal sequence per user or namespace for incremental sync.
apiNotes: POST /uploads creates a resumable session and scoped part URLs.
POST /uploads/{id}/complete validates parts before publishing a version.
GET /changes?cursor=... returns ordered metadata mutations.
keyTradeoffs: Whole-file objects simplify storage; chunking improves resume and deduplication but adds manifests and garbage collection.
Strong metadata consistency prevents conflicting names but may add coordination.
Direct object-store transfer reduces server load while requiring carefully scoped credentials.
failureModes: An upload completes in object storage but metadata publication fails.
Orphaned multipart uploads consume capacity.
Permission revocation races with cached download authorization.
Concurrent renames create confusing device state.
extensions: How would collaborative editing differ from file synchronization?
How would client-side encryption affect preview and deduplication?
How would legal retention interact with deletion?
interviewChecklist: Covered orphan cleanup and version durability.

title: Search Autocomplete
summary: Return useful query suggestions under tight latency and continuous update requirements.
prompt: Design an autocomplete service that returns query suggestions as a user types.
clarifyingQuestions: Are suggestions global, personalized, or both?
How fresh must trending queries be?
Which languages and typo behavior are required?
What unsafe or private queries must be filtered?
functionalRequirements: Return a small ranked list for a normalized prefix.
Ingest approved query signals and content terms.
Remove unsafe, sensitive, or legally restricted suggestions.
nonFunctionalRequirements: Responses should fit an interactive typing latency budget.
The service should degrade safely when fresh trend data is unavailable.
Updates should not require blocking the query path.
scaleAssumptions: Example interview assumption: 200 thousand prefix requests per second at peak.
Assume short prefixes are disproportionately hot.
Define vocabulary size and language count before estimating index memory.
capacityDiscussion: Estimate QPS from keystrokes per search session, not just completed searches.
Use prefix popularity to reason about edge and service caches.
Estimate index size from normalized terms, prefixes or trie nodes, and ranking metadata.

coreComponents.name: Suggestion API
coreComponents.purpose: Normalizes prefixes and returns filtered ranked candidates.

coreComponents.name: Serving index
coreComponents.purpose: Stores prefix-to-candidate structures optimized for reads.

coreComponents.name: Signal pipeline
coreComponents.purpose: Aggregates approved frequency and trend signals.

coreComponents.name: Index builder
coreComponents.purpose: Produces versioned serving snapshots or incremental updates.

coreComponents.name: Policy filter
coreComponents.purpose: Applies safety, privacy, and regional exclusions.

dataModelNotes: Store normalized suggestion text, score features, language, and policy state.
A trie is one option; sorted term ranges or finite-state structures may fit different constraints.
Version indexes to permit atomic rollout and rollback.
apiNotes: GET /suggest?q=prefix&locale=... returns bounded candidates.
Do not send analytics synchronously from the response path.
Internal index publication should expose version and readiness.
keyTradeoffs: Precomputing top candidates per prefix speeds reads but increases build size and update cost.
Personalization can improve relevance while increasing privacy and cache fragmentation.
Frequent incremental updates improve freshness but complicate consistency across replicas.
failureModes: A bad signal spike promotes abusive content.
Index rollout leaves replicas on incompatible versions.
Very short prefixes cause hot partitions.
Unicode normalization creates duplicate or missing suggestions.
extensions: How would typo tolerance change candidate generation?
Where could personalization be added without exposing private history?
How would you test trend freshness safely?
interviewChecklist: Handled hot prefixes and safe fallback.

title: Web Crawler
summary: Fetch a large URL frontier politely, avoid duplicate work, and publish durable crawl results.
prompt: Design a distributed crawler that discovers and fetches public web pages while respecting host-level politeness rules.
clarifyingQuestions: What portion of the web and which content types are in scope?
How frequently should known pages be revisited?
How strict are robots and per-host rate policies?
Is the output raw content, extracted text, or both?
functionalRequirements: Accept seed URLs and discover new links.
Schedule eligible URLs without duplicate concurrent fetches.
Fetch content under per-host policy and persist results and metadata.
nonFunctionalRequirements: No host should receive traffic above its configured politeness budget.
The frontier must recover after worker or coordinator failure.
Sustained discovery must not create unbounded queues.
scaleAssumptions: Example interview assumption: fetch 500 million pages per day across many hosts.
Assume response sizes and host latency have long-tailed distributions.
Define recrawl horizon and retained content versions before sizing storage.
capacityDiscussion: Estimate fetch concurrency from target pages per second and average response latency.
Size network and object storage from response bytes, compression, and retention.
Use distinct limits for global throughput, per-host scheduling, and frontier growth.

coreComponents.name: URL frontier
coreComponents.purpose: Stores eligible future work ordered by host and schedule.

coreComponents.name: Politeness scheduler
coreComponents.purpose: Leases work while enforcing host-specific next-fetch time.

coreComponents.name: Fetch workers
coreComponents.purpose: Resolve, request, validate, and record responses.

coreComponents.name: Deduplication service
coreComponents.purpose: Reduces repeated URL and content processing.

coreComponents.name: Extraction pipeline
coreComponents.purpose: Parses content and emits newly discovered links.

dataModelNotes: Normalize URLs carefully but retain the fetched canonical form.
Partition frontier ownership by host to localize politeness state.
Track leases with expiry so abandoned work can be retried safely.
apiNotes: An internal enqueue operation should be idempotent for a normalized URL and crawl generation.
Workers acknowledge durable results before leases are retired.
Operational APIs should expose per-host backlog and blocked reasons.
keyTradeoffs: Aggressive URL deduplication saves work but canonicalization can merge distinct resources.
Central scheduling simplifies politeness while limiting scale; host-sharded scheduling distributes both.
Recrawl prioritization trades freshness against coverage.
failureModes: DNS or network errors trigger synchronized retries against one host.
A crawler trap produces infinite URL variants.
Slow hosts hold worker capacity without timeouts.
Extraction outruns fetching and grows the frontier indefinitely.
extensions: How would content fingerprints detect mirrors?
How would change frequency guide recrawl?
How would regional fetchers share host policy?
interviewChecklist: Separated frontier, scheduling, fetching, and extraction.

title: Metrics Platform
summary: Ingest, aggregate, retain, and query operational time-series data under bursty cardinality.
prompt: Design a platform that collects service metrics and supports dashboards and alerts over recent and historical time windows.
clarifyingQuestions: Which metric types and query functions are required?
What ingest-to-query and alert latency is acceptable?
How long is raw resolution retained?
How should high-cardinality labels be controlled?
functionalRequirements: Ingest timestamped metric samples with bounded labels.
Query time ranges with filters and aggregations.
Evaluate alert rules and retain downsampled history.
nonFunctionalRequirements: Ingestion should survive regional bursts without unlimited buffering.
Recent dashboards should remain available during background compaction.
Tenant isolation and cardinality limits must protect shared capacity.
scaleAssumptions: Example interview assumption: 5 million samples per second with a defined retention policy.
Model active series cardinality separately from raw sample rate.
State the allowed late-arrival window before designing aggregation.
capacityDiscussion: Estimate daily compressed bytes from sample rate and encoding assumptions.
Calculate memory pressure from active series metadata and write buffers.
Compare raw, rolled-up, and replicated storage tiers by retention.

coreComponents.name: Ingest gateways
coreComponents.purpose: Authenticate, validate labels, and batch samples.

coreComponents.name: Partitioned write log
coreComponents.purpose: Buffers durable ordered streams for consumers.

coreComponents.name: Time-series writers
coreComponents.purpose: Encode samples into time-partitioned storage.

coreComponents.name: Query coordinator

coreComponents.name: Rule evaluator
coreComponents.purpose: Runs alert queries on bounded schedules.

dataModelNotes: A series identity derives from metric name plus normalized label set.
Partition by tenant and series hash, then segment by time.
Keep an index from label matchers to series IDs with explicit cardinality controls.

Query APIs need bounded range, resolution, and result limits.
Alert evaluation should reuse query semantics but have separate capacity.
keyTradeoffs: Long raw retention improves diagnosis but dominates cost.
Pre-aggregation speeds common dashboards but cannot answer every later question.
Write availability during overload may require sampling or explicit rejection.

A partition falls behind and recent queries become uneven.
Compaction competes with foreground reads.
Alert evaluation retries create duplicate notifications.

How would exemplar traces connect to a series?
How would cross-region disaster recovery work?

title: Ticket Reservation System
summary: Reserve scarce inventory without overselling while keeping browse traffic responsive.
prompt: Design a ticketing service where users browse events, temporarily hold seats, and complete purchases without overselling.
clarifyingQuestions: Are seats assigned or is inventory pooled by section?
How long does a hold last?
What payment behavior and refund scope are required?
How should extremely popular on-sales control admission?
functionalRequirements: Browse events and current seat availability.
Create an expiring hold on available inventory.
Confirm a hold after successful payment.
Release expired or failed holds.
nonFunctionalRequirements: Confirmed inventory must never exceed available inventory.
Browse traffic should not contend with the critical reservation path.
Retries across payment and confirmation must not double-charge or double-book.
scaleAssumptions: Example interview assumption: a popular event draws one million users within several minutes.
Assume writes concentrate on a small inventory set while catalog reads are broad.
Define hold duration and payment latency before estimating locked or reserved inventory.
capacityDiscussion: Estimate browse QPS separately from hold attempts and successful purchases.
Model contention per event or section rather than spreading a global average.
Use an admission queue to bound critical-path concurrency during spikes.

coreComponents.name: Catalog service
coreComponents.purpose: Serves event and seat-map metadata from cacheable views.

coreComponents.name: Admission controller
coreComponents.purpose: Bounds entry to hot on-sales.

coreComponents.name: Inventory service
coreComponents.purpose: Serializes hold and confirmation transitions per inventory partition.

coreComponents.name: Hold expiry worker
coreComponents.purpose: Releases inventory after durable deadlines.

coreComponents.name: Payment coordinator
coreComponents.purpose: Coordinates idempotent payment and booking completion.

dataModelNotes: Model each seat or inventory bucket as a state machine with versioned transitions.
A hold records owner, inventory, deadline, and idempotency key.
Keep payment attempt state separate from inventory state and reconcile ambiguous outcomes.
apiNotes: POST /holds uses an idempotency key and returns a durable expiry.
POST /holds/{id}/confirm consumes the hold once.
Availability responses should declare whether they are approximate or authoritative.
keyTradeoffs: Strong per-seat coordination protects correctness but limits hot-partition throughput.
Cached availability improves browsing but can be stale; the hold operation remains authoritative.
Waiting rooms improve stability and fairness while adding product complexity.
failureModes: Payment succeeds but confirmation response is lost.
Expiry processing pauses and inventory remains held too long.
Cache shows seats that another user just reserved.
A hot event overwhelms one database partition.
extensions: How would general-admission inventory differ?
How would seat transfers work?
How would fairness and bot mitigation affect admission?
